design_detail: Multisite prospective observational cohort (the Stay Safe Study, an ancillary study of the HEALing Communities Study), recruited May to December 2023 at fixed and mobile sites of 14 community harm-reduction organizations that distribute fentanyl test strips (FTS) in Kentucky (5), New York (3) and Ohio (6). Exposure: self-reported FTS use in the 30 days before baseline (yes or no), measured once. Follow-up: four weekly surveys over 28 days (at most 37), using a modified timeline followback to record, for each day with drug use, strip use, drugs used, eight overdose risk-reduction behaviours and nonfatal overdose. Primary outcome: a daily composite score (0–15) of the number and frequency of the eight behaviours; secondary outcomes: the count of behaviours, each behaviour and self-reported nonfatal overdose. Population-averaged generalized estimating equations with prespecified baseline and time-varying covariates; STROBE reporting. Appraised with ROBINS-I because using test strips is an intervention (topic instruction; METHODS §5.3). Strip results were not analysed.
can_establish: Whether people who already used fentanyl test strips, recruited at strip-distributing harm-reduction sites in three US states in 2023, reported more overdose risk-reduction behaviours, and more or fewer nonfatal overdoses, over the next four weeks than people at the same sites who did not, after adjustment for measured differences.
cannot_establish: Whether using test strips causes people to adopt those behaviours or prevents overdose (strip use was chosen by participants who already reported more risk reduction at baseline, outcomes were self-reported and strip results were not analysed), anything about fatal overdose, or what happens among people outside harm-reduction services.

sample.recruitment: Fixed and mobile harm-reduction sites of 14 community partner organizations distributing FTS in Kentucky, New York and Ohio, May to December 2023 (Methods › Setting; Methods › Study Design, 1st paragraph); written consent on an electronic tablet; compensation up to $250 for screening, baseline and weekly surveys, paid for each survey started (Methods › Study Design, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or older; self-assessed ability to read and speak English; able to consent; living in Kentucky, New York or Ohio and planning to stay during follow-up; past 30-day use of heroin, fentanyl, cocaine, methamphetamine, or non-prescribed opioids, benzodiazepines or stimulants. Enrolment required starting the baseline survey; the analysed sample required self-reported drug use on at least 1 day and at least 2 completed weekly surveys during follow-up (Methods › Participants).
sample.demographics: Median age 41 (IQR 34–48); 369 male (50.4%); of 722 with race recorded, 587 White (81.3%), 64 Black or African American (8.9%) and 71 other (9.8%); 64 of 724 Hispanic or Latino (8.8%); 391 of 715 unemployed (54.7%); Kentucky 254, New York 162, Ohio 316. Past 30 days: injection 491 (67.1%), fentanyl 489 of 698 (70.1%), heroin 511 of 727 (70.3%), methamphetamine 442 of 725 (61.0%), overdose 168 of 712 (23.6%) (Table 2).
sample.attrition: 424 of 1156 enrolled participants (36.7%) were not analysed because they reported no drug use during follow-up or completed fewer than 2 weekly surveys (editors' calculation; reasons in the flow diagram, an image not read; included and excluded participants compared in eTable 2, not read). Adjusted models used 677 to 690 participants (Table 3). Anonymity prevented knowing why people were lost, including whether any fatal overdoses occurred (Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Participants were clients of harm-reduction sites that distribute strips, whom the authors call not representative of all people who use drugs (Strengths and Limitations, 2nd paragraph); strip use (56.6%) was far above the median uptake of 19% in the literature cited (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). The exposure is prevalent strip use, not new use. Participants using strips already reported more risk-reduction behaviours at baseline (Results › Baseline Characteristics, 3rd paragraph), were more often from Ohio and White, and more often used fentanyl, heroin, methamphetamine and opioid–stimulant combinations and injected (Table 2).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported FTS use in the past 30 days, asked once at baseline; non-response, 'don't know' and 'prefer not to answer' were classed as no use (Methods › Exposure › Baseline FTS Use). The number of times strips were used each day during follow-up was recorded as a time-varying characteristic (Methods › Characteristics Varying Over Time). Strip results were not analysed; the authors defer that to future work (Discussion, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the exposure. Drug categories and injection were recorded daily and used as covariates.
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded: past 30-day use of eight drug classes at baseline (Table 2) and a daily drug category (opioids only; stimulants only; opioids and stimulants; benzodiazepines; none or unknown), used as a time-varying covariate (Methods › Characteristics Varying Over Time).

comparison.controls: People recruited at the same sites who reported no FTS use in the 30 days before baseline, including those who did not answer (n = 318).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured or not adjusted, as far as the main text states: prior engagement with harm-reduction services (authors' limitation), risk perception, the baseline level of the outcome behaviours (higher in the strip group; eTable 4, not read), harm-reduction messaging, which varied by site, and behavioural intent.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: All participants used drugs; the comparison group less often used fentanyl, heroin and methamphetamine and less often injected (Table 2).

outcomes.instruments: Weekly surveys with a modified timeline followback (refs. 17–18). Eight behaviours chosen by the authors from the literature (Table 1): someone else present when using; naloxone nearby; testing the strength of drugs before use; using drugs slowly; asking someone to check on you; using by a non-injection route (smoking, snorting, sniffing, swallowing or anal use); watching someone use the same drugs first; throwing out drugs that were bad or not as expected. Nonfatal overdose: a time in the past week when the participant lost consciousness and someone had to revive them (Methods › Nonfatal Overdose).
outcomes.validity_norms: The composite score is the authors' own; its validity and reliability are not reported. Behavioural intent was not measured (authors' limitation). Table 1's notes, read in the PubMed Central copy by the second reader, give the scoring (always 2, sometimes 1, never 0; throwing out bad drugs 1 or 0) and define testing the strength of drugs as trying a small amount first, and using slowly as spacing use out over time.
outcomes.operationalization: Daily composite: each behaviour rated always, sometimes or never on each drug-use day and summed across the eight, range 0–15, with discarding counting 0 or 1 because always discarding means no use that day; secondary analyses collapse always and sometimes into yes (Methods › Variables and Measurement › Outcomes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Eleven outcomes (composite score, count, eight behaviours, nonfatal overdose), each unadjusted and adjusted; the authors call all P values descriptive (Methods › Statistical Analysis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable: all outcomes were self-reported by participants who knew their own strip use.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 3, adjusted estimates unless stated. Composite score: difference 0.86 (95% CI 0.34–1.38; n = 684), mean 7.37 (6.63–8.11) in the strip group versus 6.51 (5.83–7.19); unadjusted 0.89 (0.44–1.35; n = 719). Editors' calculation: 0.86 is 5.7% of the 0–15 range and 13% above the comparison group's mean. Behaviour count: RR 1.11 (1.04–1.19). Individual behaviours (RR): naloxone nearby 1.10 (1.04–1.18); testing the strength of drugs before use 1.41 (1.24–1.61); asking someone to check 1.26 (1.10–1.45); throwing out bad or unexpected drugs 1.50 (1.12–2.01; unadjusted 1.27, 0.98–1.66); watching someone use the same drugs first 1.19 (1.04–1.36); someone else present 1.04 (0.99–1.09); using slowly 1.10 (0.99–1.22); non-injection route 0.86 (0.79–0.94). Nonfatal overdose: unadjusted RR 2.06 (1.09–3.89; n = 710), adjusted 1.20 (0.70–2.06; n = 677), mean daily risk 0.02 (0.01–0.03) in both groups; the association was modified by age in adjusted analyses (P = .02), the ratio decreasing with age (eFigure 5, not read).
analysis.covariates: Prespecified for each outcome (Methods › Covariates). Behaviour models (Table 3, note d): baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity, sex, education, employment, ever having received strip instructions and past 30-day overdose, plus daily drug category, study week and part of the week. Nonfatal-overdose model (note g): baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity and sex, plus daily drug category, study week, part of the week, the composite risk-reduction score and the number of times strips were used. Injecting entered neither (notes read in the PubMed Central copy, PMC12076174, by the second reader). Not adjusted in any model: the baseline level of the outcome behaviours.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; covariates are said to have been prespecified before analysis on the basis of the design and expert opinion. The Stay Safe Study protocol (Pro0006830) and the parent HEALing Communities Study protocol were approved by Advarra; the parent study's protocol is published (refs. 15–16).
analysis.selective_reporting: All eight behaviours and the overdose outcome are reported, unadjusted and adjusted. Interaction terms were tested but only the age interaction for overdose is reported. The analysis by strip result is announced as future work.
analysis.power: The authors state the sample was powered for the primary objective; no calculation is shown in the main text. With a mean daily overdose risk of 0.02, the adjusted risk ratio is imprecise (0.70–2.06).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Over four weeks, participants who already used test strips at baseline reported a composite risk-reduction score 0.86 points higher on a 0–15 scale (about 13% above the comparison group's mean) and more of five of the eight behaviours, but less use of non-injection routes; they had also reported more of these behaviours at baseline. Self-reported nonfatal overdose did not differ after adjustment (RR 1.20, 0.70–2.06), an interval compatible with a 30% reduction or a doubling; unadjusted, it was about twice as high in the strip group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points say the findings demonstrate “the role of FTS as a harm reduction strategy among PWUD” (Key Points › Meaning), and the Discussion that they counter the claim that strips enable fentanyl use (Discussion, 1st paragraph). The abstract's conclusion is more careful: people who use strips may also engage in a broader set of harm-reduction strategies. The design compares people who chose to use strips with people who did not, with self-reported outcomes and baseline differences in the same behaviours, so it shows co-occurrence, not a role of strips. For overdose, “no difference” (abstract) and the suggestion that strips alone may be insufficient to reduce overdose rates (Conclusions) are read from an imprecise null.

timeline.event: Krieger et al. (2018), young adults in the United States, and Karamouzian et al. (2018), a Vancouver supervised injection facility: earlier single-site studies cited by the authors (refs. 8, 51); the latter read in this batch (card sc_karamouzian_2018).
Peiper et al. (2019): strip distribution at a syringe services programme in the southeastern United States (ref. 9); not read.
Green et al. (2020): laboratory sensitivity and specificity of fentanyl strips, cited for the strips' high sensitivity (ref. 11).
Lockwood et al. (2021): high concentrations of stimulants and cutting agents cause false positives on fentanyl strips (ref. 12, cited; not read).
Maghsoudi et al. (2022), systematic review of drug checking services to 2019, not cited here (read in this batch; card sc_maghsoudi_2022).
Recruitment and data collection, May to December 2023.

Kutscher et al. (2024), a scoping review of fentanyl strips, cited for acceptability, associated behaviours and a median uptake of 19% (ref. 14); Zibbell et al. (2024), baseline findings of the South Atlantic Fentanyl Test Strip Study (ref. 52); neither read.

replication.where_it_stands: The largest prospective study of strip use and self-reported behaviour among the papers read. Its behaviour association agrees with the smaller, mostly cross-sectional studies the authors cite (summarized in a scoping review not read), and its null overdose result sits beside the crude association of intended dose reduction with lower overdose odds reported by Karamouzian et al. (2018); neither design can show an effect of strips. The authors' planned analysis of how strip results affect behaviour has not been read.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial, individual or cluster (by site or community), of offering test strips with instruction against usual services among people not yet using strips, measuring behaviours before and after and overdose from emergency, hospital and death records; failing that, a cohort of people starting to use strips (an incident-use design), adjusted for baseline behaviours and analysed by strip result.

domains.note: Adjustment differed by outcome (Table 3, notes d and g, PubMed Central copy): the behaviour models included state, demographics, education, employment, strip instructions, past overdose and daily drug category, but not injecting or the baseline level of the same behaviours; the overdose model included state, demographics and daily drug category but not injecting, past overdose or strip instructions, and it also included strip use and the risk-reduction score during follow-up, which may carry part of any effect. Prior harm-reduction engagement and risk perception were not measured; the strip group already reported more risk reduction at baseline. The crude overdose risk ratio of 2.06 falling to 1.20 after adjustment shows strong confounding by risk, possibly with over-adjustment as well.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Prevalent strip use among clients of strip-distributing sites; the analysed sample (732 of 1156) required at least 2 weekly surveys and a drug-use day, conditions met only after follow-up began.
Self-reported past 30-day use, measured once; non-response and 'don't know' classed as no use; frequency of use and results not used.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Exposure fixed at baseline while strip use during follow-up varied (recorded daily) and harm-reduction messaging varied by site; people in the comparison group may have started using strips during follow-up.

36.7% of enrolled participants were not analysed and up to 7.5% of the analysed sample dropped from the adjusted models (677 of 732); reasons for loss are unknown and may include fatal overdose; a missing-at-random mixed model for the composite score gave negligible differences.

All outcomes self-reported weekly by participants who knew their own strip use, with social desirability and recall bias (authors' limitation); the composite score is unvalidated; testing the strength of drugs is defined in Table 1's note as trying a small amount first, so it does not overlap with strip testing.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: No registration; 11 outcomes, unadjusted and adjusted, without correction for multiplicity; the covariates of each model appear only in the table notes; only one of the tested interactions is reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I judges whether the study can estimate the effect of using test strips. It shows co-occurrence rather than an effect: strip use was chosen by people who already reported more risk reduction, outcomes were self-reported, a third of enrolled participants were not analysed, and residual confounding could plausibly explain a difference of 0.86 points on a 0–15 scale. No domain is judged critical, because the design is prospective and the main measured confounders were adjusted for. Citable for: in 2023, among clients of harm-reduction sites in Kentucky, New York and Ohio, people reporting strip use also reported somewhat more risk-reduction behaviours over the next four weeks (adjusted difference 0.86 on 0–15) and less non-injection use, with no clear difference in self-reported nonfatal overdose (adjusted RR 1.20, 0.70–2.06). Not citable for: strips causing behaviour change, strips preventing or failing to prevent overdose, or the effect of strip results.

key_findings.finding: Stay Safe Study, ancillary to the HEALing Communities Study: 1156 people enrolled at 14 strip-distributing harm-reduction organizations in Kentucky, New York and Ohio, May to December 2023; 732 analysed (drug use on at least 1 day and at least 2 weekly surveys), of whom 414 (56.6%) reported strip use in the 30 days before baseline and 318 did not.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Design, Setting, and Participants; Methods › Setting; Results, 1st paragraph; Results › Baseline Characteristics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: 424 enrolled participants (36.7%) were not analysed (editors' calculation); the flow diagram is an image and was not read.

key_findings.finding: Baseline differences, strip group versus comparison group (Table 2): Ohio 48.6% versus 36.2% and New York 18.1% versus 27.4% (P = .001); White 85.8% versus 75.4% and Black 6.1% versus 12.5% (P = .001); Hispanic 5.6% versus 13.0% (P = .001); past 30-day fentanyl 78.2% versus 59.2%, heroin 76.8% versus 61.8%, methamphetamine 64.5% versus 56.4%, opioids with stimulants 65.7% versus 48.4%, injection 75.1% versus 56.6%; ever received strip instructions 76.2% versus 40.6%; past 30-day overdose 26.0% versus 20.5% (P = .10). Age, sex, education and employment did not differ.

At baseline the strip group already had a higher mean composite score and number of risk-reduction behaviours over the past 30 days and a higher prevalence of nearly every behaviour across most drug categories, except non-injection use, which was more common in the comparison group; smoking was more prevalent in the comparison group.
key_findings.note: The values are in eTables 3–5 (Supplement 1, not read).

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome: adjusted difference in the mean daily composite score 0.86 (95% CI 0.34–1.38; n = 684; P = .001), 7.37 (6.63–8.11) in the strip group versus 6.51 (5.83–7.19); unadjusted 0.89 (0.44–1.35; n = 719). Count of behaviours: adjusted rate ratio 1.11 (1.04–1.19).
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose Risk Reduction Behaviors › Mean Daily Composite Score; Mean Daily Rate of Behaviors; Table 3
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 0.86 is 5.7% of the 0–15 range and 13% above the comparison group's mean.

key_findings.finding: Individual behaviours, adjusted risk ratios for the strip group: naloxone nearby 1.10 (1.04–1.18); testing the strength of drugs before use 1.41 (1.24–1.61); asking someone to check on them 1.26 (1.10–1.45); throwing out bad or unexpected drugs 1.50 (1.12–2.01; unadjusted 1.27, 0.98–1.66); watching someone use the same drugs first 1.19 (1.04–1.36); someone else present 1.04 (0.99–1.09); using slowly 1.10 (0.99–1.22); smoking, snorting, sniffing, swallowing or anal use 0.86 (0.79–0.94).
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose Risk Reduction Behaviors › Mean Daily Probability of Each Behavior; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Self-reported nonfatal overdose: unadjusted risk ratio 2.06 (1.09–3.89; n = 710) for the strip group; adjusted 1.20 (0.70–2.06; n = 677), with a mean daily risk of 0.02 (0.01–0.03) in both groups. In adjusted analyses the association was modified by age (P = .02), the ratio decreasing as age increased.
key_findings.locator: Results › Overdose Risk Reduction Behaviors › Mean Daily Risk of Self-Reported Nonfatal Overdose; Table 3
key_findings.note: The age-specific estimates are in eFigure 5 (not read).

key_findings.finding: Measures: eight behaviours chosen by the authors from the literature, each rated always, sometimes or never on every drug-use day and summed to a 0–15 daily score (discarding counts 0 or 1); nonfatal overdose = losing consciousness and needing to be revived; exposure = self-reported strip use in the past 30 days at baseline, with non-response and 'don't know' coded as no use.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Variables and Measurement › Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Nonfatal Overdose; Exposure › Baseline FTS Use; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Analysis: population-averaged generalized estimating equations with covariates prespecified for each outcome. The table notes give two sets: for the behaviour outcomes (Table 3, note d), baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity, sex, education, employment, ever having received strip instructions and past 30-day overdose, plus daily drug category, study week and part of the week; for nonfatal overdose (note g), baseline strip use, state, age, race, ethnicity and sex, plus daily drug category, study week, part of the week, the composite risk-reduction score and the number of times strips were used. Injecting entered neither. Models: normal with identity link and compound symmetry for the composite score; Poisson with log link, with compound symmetry or first-order autoregressive structure, for the count, the single behaviours and overdose. A missing-at-random mixed model for the composite score gave negligible differences.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Covariates; Sociodemographic and Drug Use Characteristics; Characteristics Varying Over Time; Statistical Analysis; Table 3, notes b and d to g (PubMed Central copy, PMC12076174)
key_findings.note: The table notes are not on the publisher page, which shows only their letters; they were read as text in the PubMed Central copy by the second reader (AI reader 147). The Methods list the covariates without saying which model used which.

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: harm-reduction clients are not representative; no data on prior harm-reduction engagement; messaging varied across sites; a mostly non-Hispanic White sample; behavioural intent not measured; four-week follow-up; self-reports subject to social desirability and recall bias; anonymity prevented knowing why people were lost, including any fatal overdoses.

Authors' conclusions: strip use was associated with more risk-reduction behaviours but not with the risk of nonfatal overdose; strips alone may be insufficient to reduce overdose rates, particularly among people with complex, high-risk drug use, and should be integrated with other harm reduction such as naloxone distribution.
key_findings.locator: Conclusions; Abstract › Conclusions and Relevance; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The Introduction states that strips detect fentanyl at approximately 20 to 200 mg/mL in under five minutes, have high sensitivity for fentanyl and analogues, and can be affected by stimulants and cutting agents (refs. 11–13).
key_findings.note: mg/mL is implausible for an immunoassay threshold; Karamouzian et al. (2018) give a detection limit of 0.13 μg/mL (sc_karamouzian_2018), so the unit is probably ng/mL (editors' reading).

key_findings.finding: The authors hypothesized that people who used strips at baseline would report more risk-reduction behaviours and a lower daily risk of nonfatal overdose during follow-up; the unadjusted overdose estimate went the other way (RR 2.06) and the adjusted one showed no clear difference (1.20).
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 4th paragraph; Results › Mean Daily Risk of Self-Reported Nonfatal Overdose

reporting_issues.issue: Introduction, 2nd paragraph: strips are said to detect fentanyl at approximately 20 to 200 mg/mL; the detection limit reported by Karamouzian et al. (2018) is 0.13 μg/mL, about a million times lower, so the unit is probably ng/mL.
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not cite this sentence for strip sensitivity.

reporting_issues.issue: The Statistical Analysis calls all P values purely descriptive, with no correction for 11 outcomes, but the Key Points describe the strip group as significantly more likely to report more behaviours, and the Results and Discussion read the overdose estimates as tests (no longer statistically significant after adjustment).
reporting_issues.consequence: Four of the five behaviour associations that exclude 1 have lower limits between 1.04 and 1.12; cite them as descriptive estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The exposure is strip use at baseline, but the adjusted nonfatal-overdose model (Table 3, note g) also includes the number of times strips were used and the composite risk-reduction score during follow-up, which come after the exposure and may lie on its path, and it leaves out injecting and past overdose; the behaviour models (note d) include neither follow-up variable. The Discussion attributes the attenuation of the overdose estimate to the strip group's concurrent risk-raising and risk-lowering behaviours, which partly describes the adjustment itself.
reporting_issues.consequence: The adjusted overdose ratio of 1.20 may be pulled towards 1 by this adjustment as well as reflecting confounding by risk; cite it with that caveat. The behaviour estimates are not affected by it, but they were not adjusted for the baseline level of the same behaviours.

reporting_issues.issue: Abstract › Results states there was no difference in nonfatal overdose, from an adjusted risk ratio of 1.20 with a 95% CI of 0.70–2.06.
reporting_issues.consequence: An absence of evidence, not evidence of no effect; claims should give the interval.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2833888 (JAMA Network Open 8(5): e2510077, published 13 May 2025; open access), reached through https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2025.10077 at the second attempt, after a check page on the first that was not interacted with: Key Points, abstract, all sections, Tables 1–3 as text (their footnotes are only in the table images and were not read), the flow-diagram caption and footnotes (the diagram is an image; its counts were not read), article information, author contributions, conflict-of-interest, funding and funder-role statements, author affiliations and the reference list. Supplement 1 (eMethods, eTables 1–5, eFigures 1–5) and Supplement 2 (data sharing statement) were not read.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 147, corrected: the Methods list the covariates, but the models differ (Table 3 notes, PMC12076174): behaviour models (d) and the nonfatal-overdose model (g) as now stated; injection entered no model; daily strip use only the overdose model; GEE specifications from notes b, e and f.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted: the first reader had not read the notes (key finding note: 'not read; could not be checked'), the saved publisher page shows separate notes for the overdose estimate (g) and the behaviour estimates (d) and says covariates were prespecified for the model of each outcome, and the second reader read the notes in the PubMed Central copy.
